prompt.context: Our client is A+Airline Co., the third largest airline in the United States by passengers carried. This week, we have been flying on our primary competitor, Gamma Airline, and we noticed something interesting: they stopped accepting cash for in-flight food and beverage services and they now only accept major credit cards.
prompt.question: The CEO of A+Airline Co. wants to know: (1) Why did Gamma Airline switch from a Cash & Card system to a Credit Card only system, and (2) Should A+Airline follow them?

clarifying_info.q: What percentage of passengers have a credit card available?
clarifying_info.a: Roughly 99% of all consumers purchase their airline tickets using a credit card, meaning all passengers on the airplane have a credit card available to them.

clarifying_info.q: What items are sold on A+Airline flights?
clarifying_info.a: Only food and alcoholic beverage items are sold on A+Airline flights.

clarifying_info.q: Does this apply to international flights as well?
clarifying_info.a: This is a US Domestic decision only. Ignore international flights.

clarifying_info.q: Has any other airline made this switch besides Gamma?
clarifying_info.a: Gamma is the only airline that has made the switch so far; however, all other airlines are evaluating the switch.

clarifying_info.q: How similar is Gamma Airline to A+Airline?
clarifying_info.a: For the purposes of this case, Gamma and A+Airline should be considered to be exactly the same in all regards.

exhibits.title: An Average A+Airline Flight
exhibits.shows: Seat and passenger data for a Boeing 737-800 including total seats, load factor by class, business vs. leisure mix, purchase rates, average spend per passenger type, and the current cash vs. card payment split for in-flight purchases.

data.note: First Class Passengers Receive Free Food & Beverage

exhibits.title: A+Airline Cash & Card Operations
exhibits.shows: Current operational details for both Cash Management and Card Management processes at A+Airline, including associated fees and staffing overhead for cash operations at airports.

framework: BEFORE vs. AFTER comparison: analyze the delta (changes) from switching from Cash & Card to Card Only — not absolute historical costs/revenues
Revenue Changes: (1) Loss of Cash-Only customers who will not convert to card, vs. (2) Potential increase in card customer spending
Cost Changes: (1) Benefit from eliminating Cash Management overhead costs, vs. (2) Incremental Credit Card processing fees
Cash Flow / TVM Changes: Impact of receiving payment faster (credit card settles same day vs. cash requires 30-day reconciliation) and working capital improvements

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the total market size in dollars for food and beverage purchases on an average flight, then determine the current cash vs. card split.
questions.guidance: Interviewee must work through all calculation steps without rounding. Steps: (1) Total passengers by class, (2) Purchasers by segment, (3) Total spend, (4) Cash vs. card allocation.

math.setup: Boeing 737-800: 200 total seats. First Class = 25% x 200 = 50 seats, 100% load = 50 passengers, all Business, Free F&B (excluded). Economy = 75% x 200 = 150 seats, 80% load = 120 passengers, 50% Business = 60, 50% Leisure = 60. Purchase rates: Business 75% of 60 = 45 purchasers; Leisure 25% of 60 = 15 purchasers. Avg spend: Business $10, Leisure $5.
steps: Economy Business purchasers: 60 x 75% = 45; spend = 45 x $10 = $450
Economy Leisure purchasers: 60 x 25% = 15; spend = 15 x $5 = $75
math.answer: Total in-flight food & beverage market per flight = $525. Cash portion = $105 (20%), Card portion = $420 (80%).

questions.prompt: We will lose 1/3 of current Cash customers after the switch. Calculate the revenue loss.
questions.guidance: Apply 1/3 loss rate to current cash purchasers (both Business and Leisure). Compute dollar loss per segment.

math.setup: Current cash purchasers: Business cash purchasers = 45 x 20% = 9; Leisure cash purchasers = 15 x 20% = 3. Lose 1/3 of each segment.
steps: Business cash customers lost: 9 x 1/3 = 3 customers; Revenue lost = 3 x $10 = $30
Leisure cash customers lost: 3 x 1/3 = 1 customer; Revenue lost = 1 x $5 = $5
Total customers lost: 3 + 1 = 4; Total revenue lost = $30 + $5 = $35
math.answer: Revenue loss = $35 per flight (3 Business + 1 Leisure customer lost). New total = $490 per flight.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, analyze the cost changes from switching to Card Only. What costs are eliminated and what new costs are incurred?
questions.guidance: Key insight: both Cash Management and Card Management carry a 2% processing fee — this is a wash. The real savings come from eliminating Cash Management overhead (7 employees per airport). Interviewer confirms total per-flight savings from eliminating cash overhead = $35/flight. Net cost change = $35 saved - $0 incremental fee = $35 net savings.

math.setup: Cash fee = 2% of cash spend. Card fee = 2% of card spend. Under Card Only, all spend is on card at 2%. Previously, cash was also at 2%. So the fee rate is identical — no change in fee expense. Overhead savings = $35 per flight (given by interviewer).
steps: Card fee on current card spend: 2% x $420 = $8.40
Card fee on previously-cash spend that converts: 2% x ($105 - $35 lost) = 2% x $70 = $1.40 (incremental fee on converted cash customers)
Net: $35 overhead savings - $1.40 incremental card fee on converted customers ≈ $33.60 net savings (casebook simplification: treat 2%/2% as wash and state $35 savings)
math.answer: The 2% fee applies equally to both cash and card management — effectively a wash. Eliminating Cash Management overhead saves $35 per flight. Net cost saving ≈ $35 per flight, which offsets the $35 revenue loss. Since cost savings go directly to the bottom line while revenue losses are top-line, the switch is financially favorable.

questions.prompt: Qualitatively, what is the impact of receiving payment 30 days sooner under a Card-Only system?
questions.guidance: Interviewee should identify Time Value of Money (TVM) and Working Capital benefits. No math required — this is a qualitative assessment.

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond the quantitative revenue and cost analysis, what are the qualitative benefits of switching to a Card-Only system?

categories.name: Time Value of Money (TVM)
ideas: Receive payment 30 days sooner than under cash reconciliation
Invest freed-up funds in interest-earning accounts
Invest in growth projects or capital expenditures
Pay off suppliers early and capture early-payment discounts
Pay down lines of credit faster, reducing interest expense

categories.name: Working Capital Improvement
ideas: Eliminate $50 per flight in 'change' tied up on aircraft
Reduce cash loss due to theft by flight crew or passengers
Reduce cash loss due to physical damage (spills, wear)
Faster settlement reduces accounts-receivable balance

categories.name: Customer Experience
ideas: Faster transaction speed improves the purchase experience for majority of passengers
Reduces frustration for economy passengers waiting in the aisle
Reduced transaction time increases the probability of purchase (fewer abandoned purchases)
Card-only removes 'guilt' effect — consumers who lack cash tend to spend less when a cash option exists, since using a card for small amounts feels awkward; removing cash option removes this friction

categories.name: Operational Simplicity
ideas: Eliminates need for 7 cash-management employees per airport
Reduces complexity of end-of-flight cash reconciliation
Lower risk of accounting errors from manual cash handling
Streamlined training for flight attendants

categories.name: Competitive & Strategic Signals
ideas: Gamma Airline has already validated the model — de-risks the decision
All other airlines are evaluating the same switch — first-mover advantage in operational efficiency
Signals modernity and alignment with cashless payment trends

recommendation: A+Airline should switch to a Credit Card only system for in-flight food and beverage purchases.

Quantitatively, the $35 per-flight revenue loss from cash-only customers who will not convert is fully offset by $35 in per-flight overhead savings from eliminating Cash Management operations; since the cost savings are bottom-line while the revenue loss is top-line, the net income impact is favorable.

Qualitatively, the switch accelerates cash collection by 30 days (TVM benefit), improves working capital by eliminating $50 per flight in circulating change, reduces theft/damage risk, and is likely to increase average transaction speed and purchase probability for the majority of customers.
risks: A small segment of passengers who genuinely carry only cash (approximately 1.3% of total passengers) will be unable to purchase, creating a negative brand experience for this group.
If credit card processing infrastructure fails mid-flight, A+Airline would have no fallback payment method.
Potential negative press or social media backlash from customers who object to the cashless policy on principle.
next_steps: Pilot the Card-Only policy on a select number of routes to measure actual customer churn and spend uplift before full rollout.
Communicate the change clearly to customers at booking and at the gate to minimize surprise and frustration.
Evaluate whether a prepaid card or voucher option should be offered at the gate for the rare cash-only traveler.
Quantify the full-year bottom-line impact across the entire domestic fleet and present to the board.
